marks.line: Hello everyone. Today, I will be demonstrating my DevOps capstone project, called ServiceDesk.
ServiceDesk is a help desk ticket management application designed to help support teams create, track, assign, and resolve support tickets.

Each ticket contains information such as the requester, category, severity, assigned person, and current status. Every ticket also has a Service Level Agreement, or SLA, deadline that is set twenty-four hours after its creation.
The main objective of this project was not just to develop an application, but to implement the complete DevOps lifecycle around it.
This includes automated testing, containerization, continuous integration and delivery, security scanning, Kubernetes deployment, infrastructure as code, and application monitoring.
Throughout this walkthrough, I will demonstrate how these components work together to make the application more reliable, secure, and easier to deploy.
The application is built using FastAPI for the backend, React and TypeScript for the frontend, and PostgreSQL for persistent data storage.
I will now demonstrate the basic ticket workflow.
First, I am creating a new ticket by entering the required details, selecting a category and severity, and submitting the form.
Once I submit it, the ticket appears in the dashboard. This demonstrates that the frontend communicates with the backend and that the ticket is stored in the database.
Next, I will change the ticket status to Pending. Notice how the dashboard statistics update to reflect the current state of the ticket queue.
The backend exposes eleven API endpoints covering ticket operations, categories, health checks, readiness checks, and application metrics.

The database also uses a relational schema in which tickets reference categories through a foreign key. This maintains referential integrity and ensures that category relationships are managed properly.
Now I will verify the statistics directly through the API.
This response provides the ticket statistics directly from the backend.

The SLA breach count is calculated using the ticket deadline and its current status. Only tickets that remain open or pending are considered for this count. A ticket that has already been resolved is not counted as an active SLA breach, even if its deadline has passed.
This demonstrates that the dashboard statistics are based on actual application logic rather than hard-coded values.
This response provides the ticket statistics directly from the backend.
The next part of the project is automated testing.
I have created a backend test suite that covers the main application functionality, API behavior, and important edge cases.
When I run the test suite, the output shows the number of tests executed and whether they passed successfully.
The project has forty tests and ninety-eight percent test coverage, according to the project's test results.
One particularly important aspect is the isolation of the test database.
In the test configuration file, the test database URL is resolved before the application is imported. The configuration also checks that the test database is not the same as the production database.
Now I will demonstrate how the application is containerized using Docker.
Docker Compose allows the required services to be started together with a single command.
The output shows the services defined in the Compose configuration and their current status.
The frontend uses a multi-stage Docker build.
In the first stage, Node.js compiles the frontend application. In the final stage, Nginx serves the compiled static files.
This approach keeps the build tools out of the production image and helps reduce the final image size.
This is the continuous integration and delivery pipeline for the project.
Whenever a change is pushed to the main branch, the workflow runs a series of automated jobs to validate the application before publishing container images.
The pipeline includes frontend build validation, backend testing, image building and security scanning, image publishing, a Docker Compose smoke test, and a final summary.
I want to highlight a failed run because it demonstrates one of the most important features of the pipeline: a failing test must prevent an unverified artifact from being published.
This run corresponds to commit `759989a`. A deliberately failing test was introduced to verify the behavior of the pipeline.
As you can see, the test job failed. The downstream image build and publishing jobs were skipped, and the Compose smoke test was skipped as well.
That distinction is important. The pipeline did not simply report a failure after publishing the image. The dependency conditions prevented those downstream jobs from running.
Now I will switch to the container registry to show how this affects the published artifacts.
The registry contains images associated with successful commits.
Each image is tagged with a Git commit SHA, which makes it possible to trace the image back to the exact source code version that produced it.
This workflow does not rely on a floating latest tag. Instead, commit-specific tags make deployments more reproducible and easier to audit.
The failed commit did not produce a published image, as verified in the registry.
Together, the GitHub Actions workflow and the registry demonstrate that the pipeline acts as a release gate and that published artifacts can be traced back to their source code.
Security scanning is another important part of this project.
The pipeline uses Trivy to scan container images for known vulnerabilities. The workflow is configured to fail when vulnerabilities meet the specified high or critical severity threshold.
I will now show the Trivy ignore configuration.
The ignore file is empty, meaning that no vulnerabilities are being suppressed through this file.
During development, I encountered two high-severity findings related to the Python dependency chain. The problem was that another dependency was restricting the version that could be installed.
Instead of suppressing the findings, I traced the dependency constraint and upgraded the package that was holding the version back.
After this change, the affected findings disappeared from the report.
Next, I will demonstrate how the application is deployed on Kubernetes using Helm.
The frontend and backend are deployed as separate workloads. Each is configured with two replicas, allowing Kubernetes to maintain multiple instances of the application.
The services use ClusterIP networking, so internal communication happens through Kubernetes services instead of requiring each pod to have a public IP address.
Ingress provides the entry point for browser traffic. The root path routes to the frontend, while the configured API path routes requests to the backend.
Helm manages the deployment as a release. The release history shows the revisions created through installation and subsequent changes, including image updates and scaling operations.
This is useful because it provides a record of deployment changes and allows us to roll back when necessary.
I will now switch to the browser to show the application through the configured Ingress hostname.
The application is accessible through the Ingress endpoint, demonstrating how browser traffic reaches the Kubernetes deployment.
I will now demonstrate pod recovery.
When a pod managed by a Deployment is deleted, Kubernetes detects that the desired number of replicas is no longer available and creates a replacement.
The application data is stored separately in PostgreSQL, so deleting a backend pod should not delete the existing tickets.
I will verify this by deleting a backend pod and checking that Kubernetes creates a replacement.
Monitoring is the next part of the project.
Prometheus collects application metrics by scraping the configured backend endpoints.
On this page, I can inspect the configured targets and check whether Prometheus is successfully collecting metrics from the application.
Both backend replicas should appear as healthy targets when the deployment is operating correctly.
Grafana provides the dashboard for visualizing these metrics.
The ServiceDesk dashboard contains twenty-three panels covering application-level behavior, including request rates, error ratios, and latency percentiles.
These metrics help us understand how the application is performing instead of looking only at the health of the underlying infrastructure.
I will now generate some traffic and show how it appears in the dashboard.
I have now sent sixty requests to the ticket API.
After the metrics collection and dashboard refresh interval, the request-rate panel should reflect the additional traffic.
The exact graph depends on the scrape interval, dashboard time range, and query window.
This project also includes infrastructure as code using Terraform.

The configuration describes a thirty-five-resource infrastructure plan, including a VPC, four subnets distributed across two availability zones, an internet gateway, NAT, route tables, security groups, an EKS cluster, and a managed node group.
I want to be transparent about the scope of this module.
I did not have access to an AWS account, so I did not apply the EKS infrastructure to a live AWS environment.
The networking portion was applied and destroyed against LocalStack, which is a local AWS service emulator. I have the Terraform state and command-line verification for that work.
However, the EKS portion was planned and validated rather than deployed, because the free LocalStack environment used for this project does not implement the required EKS API.
I have documented this limitation in the README.
I believe it is important to distinguish between infrastructure that has actually been deployed and infrastructure that has only been planned and validated.

To conclude, this project gave me practical experience across the full DevOps lifecycle, from application development and automated testing to container security, CI/CD, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, and monitoring.
There are two improvements I would prioritize next.
First, I would introduce an advisory lock around database migration execution to prevent multiple replicas from racing during initial startup.
Second, I would validate and deploy the Terraform EKS configuration in a real AWS account when the necessary access is available.
One of my biggest lessons was that a deployment environment can expose problems that do not appear in local testing.
I encountered issues involving non-root container execution, binaries with file capabilities, and proxy Host header and SNI behavior.
These experiences taught me that passing tests is essential, but portability and real deployment behavior must also be verified.
Thank you for watching my ServiceDesk DevOps capstone demonstration.
